en: Salutations to the illustrious Great Preceptor of the Upanishads.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 2, Verse 9.
The Second Daily Lesson.

Therefore, in this context, for the purpose of excluding error (*viparyaya*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*) under the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), the qualification "concordant with discourse as it actually exists" (*yathāvasthitavyavahārānuguṇa*) is included in the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even under the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), the cognition that has entered into the causal complex [of that erroneous experience] is designated by the word "that" (*tat*);
and since it is established in the world that such [cognition] is not valid in that instance, it must indeed be excluded.
Even there, the correspondence with reality is not undermined in each individual part.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 2, Verse 10.
The examination of error.
In that regard, according to the first position, error (*viparyaya*) is the determination of one thing as being otherwise;

however, according to the second position, it is the determination of a specific contradictory attribute while there is a general manifestation of the locus (*dharmī*), yet without the apprehension of its contradiction.
And this [erroneous cognition] is of many kinds, because of the manifestation of one or many contradictory particulars (*viśeṣa*).
Among these, the manifestation of a single particular is, for example, "the conch is yellow," and so forth.
The manifestation of many particulars is, for example, that of the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*), such as "the one is both different and non-different," and so forth.
For the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is characterized as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent;

such a reversal, consisting of multiple mutually contradictory attributes, arises from doubt. When there is no misconception regarding mutual contradiction, there occurs a determinative synthesis (*samuccitādhyavasāya*) of these [attributes] in combination.

As for the manifestation of multiple non-contradictory attributes when there is a contradiction in properties (*dharma-virodha*), it is, for example, the perception of smallness, duality, and so forth, with respect to the moon which is qualified by vastness and oneness.

Some, however, distinguish between *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) and *viparītakhyāti* (erroneous apprehension) based on the distinction between a different property (*dharmāntara*) and a different substratum (*dharmin*), respectively; they apply these terms to cases such as the delusions of a yellow conch-shell and a rope-snake.
And it is proclaimed that for both of these, *rajas* and *tamas* are the root cause.
“That intellect by which one perceives dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, O Pārtha, is of the nature of passion (rājasī).”
“That intellect which, enveloped by darkness, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and all things in a perverted manner, O Pārtha, is tāmasī.”
Thus [it is said].
Although in an error such as that of a rope-snake, there is indeed the superimposition of a property like "snakeness"— which is the opposite of a property like "rope-ness"— nevertheless,
because it is an internal factor as a property that defines the very nature [of the substrate], it is designated as the "contrariety of the substrate" (dharmivaiparītya).
In contrast, whiteness and the like merely serve to specify a nature already defined.

In the *Vivaraṇa*, however, it is stated as follows: "Ignorance is threefold: ignorance of essential nature (*svarūpājñāna*), erroneous cognition (*anyathājñāna*), and contrary cognition (*viparītajñāna*)."
Non-apprehension of the true nature (*svarūpājñāna*) is the non-cognition of a thing.
Misapprehension (*anyathājñāna*) is the appearance of a thing as another thing,
such as the cognition of mother-of-pearl as silver.
Misconception (*viparītajñāna*), however, is the establishing of a thing as being otherwise through fallacious arguments when it is appearing exactly as it is;

for example, the establishing of non-error by means of bad reasoning regarding the self (*ātman*) even though it appears as the knower and as "I"—this is what happens for those of wrong views (*kudṛś*).

The arising of error occurs as the case may be, through such factors as unrighteousness (*adharma*), defects of the sense organs (*indriyadoṣa*), the practice of fallacious reasoning (*dustarkābhyāsa*), the pursuit of false pervasions (*durvyāptyanusaṃdhāna*), and hearing the words of deceivers, all of which are conjoined with the failure to grasp reality (*tattvāgraha*).
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 11.
The definition of doubt.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the manifestation of multiple particulars that are not apprehended as being in opposition [to one another]—despite the fact that their mutual opposition has been apprehended—while there is a manifestation of a common substratum (*sāmānyadharmī*).

For example: when there is the mere perception of an upright object, there occurs the manifestation of "post-ness" (*sthāṇutva*) and "man-ness" (*puruṣatva*), which are mutually clearly opposed and whose opposition is not yet reconciled by a synthesis (*ananusaṃdhīyamāna*); thus: "Is this a post or a man? (*ayaṃ sthāṇur vā puruṣo vā*).
If their mutual contradiction were not apprehended, there would be no alternation between them;

for that very reason, some say, "In this case, there is a sequence of flickering like the momentum of a swing," because it is contrary to experience for two mutually exclusive things to be presented simultaneously by a single cognition.

In this regard, even the passage from the *Ātmasiddhi*—“For a firm conjunction of consciousness with an object is certainty (niścaya); while a simultaneous, non-firm conjunction of that very [consciousness] with many [objects] is doubt (saṃśaya)” —is not contradictory;
otherwise, it would be impossible to describe the firm or non-firm contact between cognition and its object.
The term "simultaneously" (*yugapat*), however, refers merely to extreme rapidity.
Even if simultaneity were admitted, there would still be a lack of firmness, which is simply a specific mode of mutual exclusion;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of doubt, such as "Is this upright or a post? and so forth.
Even though such doubt may arise for some regarding things that are not contradictory—due to perceiving a contradiction rooted in factors such as non-dharma—for example:
"Is the self knowledge or the knower? or "Is knowledge a property (dharma) or the substratum (dharmin)? and so forth;
Nevertheless, even in that case, there is indeed a mutual exclusion based on conceit (*abhimānika*).
And its arising occurs, as the case may be, from these two uncommon causes—namely, similarity (*sāmānya*) and conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*)—conjoined with demerit (*adharma*) and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Tattvaratnākara*: "What is this doubt, and how many kinds are there?"
"Doubt is the appearance of multiple contradictory particulars regarding a single substratum (*dharmin*);
and it is of two kinds," and so forth.
In this context, "common property" (*samānadharmah*) refers to a shared characteristic (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).
An example produced by that [doubt] is: "Is it a post or a person? since there is no distinction in their verticality.
Here, "conflict" (*vipratipatti*) refers to the presentation of multiple contradictory indicators whose relative strength is not being apprehended.
And that conflict is of many kinds, based on the distinction between two, three, four, or more indicators, which take the form of appearances belonging to both similar and dissimilar classes.
Doubt arises from conflicting views regarding perception and its semblance, as follows: the surface of a mirror appears with one's face to the eye, yet it appears otherwise to the sense of touch;
thus, one wonders, "Is this [surface] with my face or without my face?"

An example of a conflict regarding inference and its fallacy is as follows: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," versus "It does not possess fire because it lacks light"; in this case, the doubt arises whether it possesses fire or does not possess fire. An example of a conflict regarding scriptural testimony is as follows: based on the designations of both difference and non-difference, the doubt arises whether the individual soul (jīva) is different from Brahman or non-different from Brahman, and so forth.

An example of contradiction between disputants is as follows: for a neutral observer who hears two statements from a Vaiśeṣika and an Upaniṣadic philosopher, there arises the doubt, "Are the sense organs material (bhautika) or derived from ego-consciousness (āhaṅkārika)?
Similarly, there is contradiction due to the statements of common folk and others: "There are fruits on the bank of the river," [and "There are no fruits on the bank of the river"].
"Whether they exist or not," and so forth.

This refers to a conflict between perception and inference, as for example: when there is the visual illusion of a yellow conch-shell, yet there is an inference of its whiteness based on its being a conch-shell;
thus one wonders, "Is this conch-shell yellow or white?"
An example of conflict between perception and scripture is: "Is the referent of the word 'I' gross or subtle?

An example of conflict between inference and scripture is: "Is the world derived from atoms as its material cause, or is it derived from Brahman as its material cause? This is the general direction [of such cases].
However, some, being confused by the mere word "disagreement" (vipratipatti), think that disagreement refers only to the disagreement among disputants; that is incorrect,
because there is no distinction [between the two].
As it is stated in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*: "Doubt is held to be threefold: from seeing a common form, from grasping multiple aspects [in a single object], and from the disputes of the learned."

This too is surely merely an imitation of others, because the second and third [alternatives] are identical, because the distinction between types of perceivers would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and because it is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*).
And here, the apprehension of multiple forms (*anekākāra*) is intended to mean the apprehension of various forms (*nānākāra*).
But there is no apprehension of a unique form excluded from many [others],
because immediately thereafter, with the words "In these objects, without distinction, there are two cognitions grasping two forms," etc., that very [point] is illustrated.
Some maintain that doubt can also arise from an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*); for example: "Is earth eternal or non-eternal, because it possesses odor?

In this case, since the possession of odor excludes [earth] from being of the nature of the eternal self (*ātman*) and so forth, it serves as a reminder of non-eternality, just like the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).

It is incorrect to claim that a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) excluded from both [the similar and dissimilar instances], like the property of being partless (*niravayavatva*), serves as a reminder of permanence through its exclusion from impermanence and so forth— just as a common property endowed with two contradictory specificities does.
For doubt does not arise there on account of the possession of odor (*gandhavattva*) and the like.

Rather, it is by means of properties such as *dravyatva* (substance-ness) that appear common to both eternal and non-eternal entities—long before there is any delay in determining the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—that [the object] is apprehended.

However, when one intends to determine one of the two alternatives by reflecting upon a distinguishing property (*viśeṣaka-dharma*), one considers only this much: that "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*) does not lead to the exclusion of either [alternative], because it is not co-present with both.
This will become clear in the refutation of the *kevalavyatirekin* [reason].
When someone might argue that "earth is either eternal or non-eternal because it possesses odor," even in that case,
the doubt remains as to whether the possession of odor is the probans for either eternity or non-eternity; and that doubt,
too, arises solely from a common property characterized by being a quality (*dharma*) and so forth.

Now, if one entertains the doubt as to whether [the object] is eternal or non-eternal by taking forward its possession of a property excluded from the eternal as the reason for non-eternality, and its possession of a property excluded from the non-eternal as the reason for eternality—
even then, this doubt is caused by two properties serving as reasons;
for there is not just a single reason here.
In that case, odor is merely a common property standing by the side; it is not the cause.
Some also include *vipratipatti* (contradictory cognition) within the category of the "common" (*samāna-dharma*).

For just as "uprightness" is common to both [the disputants], so too are such properties as being accepted by the proponent common; or else, because the subject (*dharmin*) which is the object of dispute, in its general form, is common to both.

Nevertheless, just as a common property (sādhāraṇadharma) serves as a reminder of both sthāṇutva and puruṣatva experienced together, so too does contradiction (vipratipatti), even though it is independent of the inference of a common property, serve as a direct reminder of those specific alternatives by being dependent upon that [common property]; thus, we have stated that there are two possibilities.
Furthermore, this [doubt] is of many kinds due to differences in the basis of its two, three, four, or more aspects;
for example: "Is this a post or a person? or "Is a jar real, unreal, indefinable, or not-indefinable? and so forth.
Likewise, [there is doubt] such as: "Are these two a post or men? or "Are these objects real, unreal, definable, or indefinable?
Furthermore, when it is established that one of two persons is a thief, there arises the doubt: "Is this one the thief, or is that one the thief?"
This, however, is a combination of two types of doubt: "Is this a thief or not?
or alternatively, "He who is the thief, is he this one or that one?"—which constitutes a single [doubt].
Alternatively, [the statement] "Is this man a thief, or is he not?"—

even though it possesses a definitive core because its intent lies either in the absence of thievery in a person distinct from both [the two mentioned], or in the thievery of one of the two, nevertheless,
since there is no determination regarding the specific identity of either of the two, in that respect it remains a doubt.

Nor is there any contradiction in a single cognition having both the nature of doubt and the nature of certainty, because even in every instance of doubt, the element of certainty regarding the locus (*dharmī*) and so forth is difficult to discard.
Furthermore, this [doubt] is of two kinds, distinguished by whether it is capable or incapable of resolving into one of the two alternatives.
The former is, for example: "Is this object, which is actually a post, a post or a person? The latter, however, is: "Is this heap of straw a young elephant or a mountain peak?"
In that regard, for those who investigate, [the decision] generally occurs first;
and for one who acts on that very basis, there is the occasional attainment of the object.

Alternatively, even for one who is inactive, acting at some point due to a second doubt or a misconception, there may be the attainment of the desired object by chance through the convergence of circumstances at that time.

Furthermore, these two—doubt and error—are to be understood as being of many kinds, based on the distinctions between the perceived nature of the general substratum (*sāmānyadharmī*) and the remembered nature of its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).

Some maintain that "non-determination" (*anadhyavasāya*)—in the form of "What is the name of this tree? and so forth—is a distinct type of cognition; however, that is untenable, because it consists essentially in a desire to know the specific details immediately following a doubt regarding those very particulars such as names.
Alternatively, due to the non-perception of a differentiator (*avacchedaka*), it is simply a doubt (*saṃśaya*) whose specific alternatives remain undetermined.

*Ūha* (presumption), however, is that very same [cognition] which, arising from the observation of many properties concomitant with one alternative—such as "this must generally be a man"—has the other alternative as its non-prominent object.
If the intention behind "this must generally be a man" is "it must be a man indeed," then it is included appropriately within perception, inference, or other means of knowledge.
As for *ūha* in the form of *tarka* (hypothetical reasoning), we shall discuss it under inference.

There are three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa), distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and verbal testimony (śabda). This was also stated by the Blessed One [Maitreya]: "Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be thoroughly understood by one who desires the establishment of the Dharma."
Thus it is said.
And the Blessed Śaunaka said: "The object of meditation is threefold, arising from perception, inference, and scripture.

And the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra), having explicitly mentioned the triad beginning with direct perception, stated: "Even though there is dispute regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this very [triad] belongs to all those means of valid cognition that are universally accepted."
"Thus, the claim that 'the reality devoid of distinctions is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)' expresses disregard for others;
and the phrase 'of all accepted means of valid cognition' indicates merely what is accepted by the opponent, since the opponent accepts six means of valid cognition."
Furthermore, the mutual distinction between perception, inference, and scripture has been clearly established in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*.

As for the commentary on the verse "From me come memory, knowledge, and their removal," which states: "Knowledge is the ascertainment of an object born of the senses, inferential marks, scripture, or yoga"—even there, the separate designation is due to the predominance of perception born of yoga;
we shall explain its subsumption [under other categories] later.

And it was stated by Śrī Viṣṇucitta in the *Prameyasaṃgraha*: "Regarding the phrase 'even though there is dispute concerning the number of means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),' the state of having three means of valid knowledge is what is taught in the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, in certain manuscripts of the *Bhāṣya*, at the point where the theory of *yathārthakhyāti* (the correspondence of cognition with its object) is being established, it says: "Or rather, what is the use of this elaborate method of demonstration?

The collection of means of valid knowledge known as perception, inference, and scripture, as well as that which is accessible through scripture—[namely, the Supreme Being] who is free from even a trace of defect and possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities—"
The reading is seen as follows: "For those who accept the Supreme Brahman as omniscient and whose will is true, what will not be accomplished? What will not be possible? and so forth.

Although it will be stated that even memory (*smṛti*), when it is in accordance with reality, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, because it is not distinct from [perception and the other sources] due to its being rooted in perception and so forth, it is not mentioned separately.

And it has been said in the *Tattvaratnākara*: "Since memories rooted in perception and the like are intended to be included within their respective sources, there is no contradiction in the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition."

And the Vedic corroboration for the number four has been shown [in the passage]: "Smṛti, perception, tradition, and inference—this is the fourfold [means of knowledge]. And that is a restatement (anuvāda) of what was previously mentioned: "Smṛti, perception, tradition, and inference constitute the fourfold [set]," because it is a restatement of the Vedas without distinguishing between perception and the others.

However, in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*, even while not accepting the authority of Smṛti, the fourfold nature of knowledge itself is stated on the basis of the difference in its instruments: "In that regard, the connection between the sense organ and the object, the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*), and the apprehension of the word... [and so forth].
Likewise:
"The manifestation of mental formations—these are the causes for the birth of cognitions."
Thus [it is said].

As for that which is stated in that very same [work]: "Self-evident proof, as well as divine perception, inference, and scripture—these five means of valid cognition reside in the hearts of Jaimini and Vyāsa."

By such statements, the separate definition of self-established perception (*svayaṃsiddhi*) and divine perception (*divya*) has been provided; this is intended to indicate the internal distinctions within the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As stated by the venerable Viṣṇucitta: “Divine perception is the yogic direct perception obtained through the grace of the Blessed Lord.”
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 12.
The definition of direct perception.
In this context, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is valid cognition that is direct.
And "directness" is a certain specific nature of cognition—whether it be of the form of a universal (*jāti*) or a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—which is personally experienced by the self.

Cognition that is devoid of being produced by a known cause or by memory is "immediate" (aparokṣa); according to this definition, there is no risk of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) or other such fallacies.
In the *Prameyasaṃgraha*, however, it is stated thus: "Direct experience is perception (*pratyakṣa*); directness is a universal (*jāti*)"—and so forth.
In the *Tattvaratnākara* as well, it is stated thus: "Perception is immediate valid cognition; and the immediacy of consciousness..."
"The exclusion of being produced by a cognition related to an object that is conventionally expressible."
Thus it is said.

And thus, mediacy (*pārokṣya*) has been explained: "Mediacy is the dependence upon the cognition of an object that is not included within the sphere of immediate experience; mediacy in inference and the like is the dependence upon signs (*liṅga*) and so forth that are not included therein. However, in the *Mānāryatattvanirṇaya*, Varadaviṣṇumiśra stated as follows: "Immediate valid cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
"We say that the immediacy (*āparokṣya*) of valid cognition consists in its quality of vivid manifestation (*viśadāvabhāsatva*). What is this so-called 'vividness' (*vaiśadya*)?
It is the capacity to manifest an object by way of its specific, unique form (*asādhāraṇākāra*)," and so forth.
Manifestness (sākṣāttva) is twofold: eternal and non-eternal.
That which resides in the eternal knowledge and so forth of the Lord (īśvara) is eternal;
however, that which resides in the knowledge of those such as ourselves is non-eternal.
The direct perception of those such as ourselves is twofold: the direct perception of yogis and the direct perception of non-yogis.
Among these, the direct perception of yogis arises from a distinguished excellence of extraordinary merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
In the state of union (*yuktāvasthā*), it is produced by the mind alone.
In the state of dissociation, however, [perception] may even be produced by the external sense organs;
and that [perception], being restricted by factors such as the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and so forth, is established solely through scripture.
It was refuted in the *Śāstrayonitva* section that perception arising merely from the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) can apprehend the Creator of the world.
This is because the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself has explicitly stated the existence of yogic perception;

furthermore, since that [perception] is possible and is rooted in the knowledge of God derived from scripture, he remained indifferent toward it, being unable to reduce it to a mere restatement of scripture.
[For instance, he argued: "Dharma and so forth must be perceptible by the senses of someone..."
Because it is an object of cognition, like a jar; or because it is not perceived by the Mīmāṃsakas.

This is because inferences such as "like our own pleasure and so forth" are fallacious due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against their contrary (*vipakṣa*), and because if one prioritizes the consequence of contradicting scripture (*āgamabādhaprasaṅga*), the matter is already settled by scripture itself.
Otherwise, what would you say in reply to a Buddhist who asserts that dharma and other such things are perceptible to the eye?

Furthermore, for one who maintains that in a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) there is the perceptuality of the object-awareness (*vyavasāya*) together with its object, how can the inference of a yogic perception distinct from that [ordinary perception] be established? For, in the case of people like us, when there is a reflective awareness of an awareness of dharma and so forth, the perceptuality of dharma and so forth would be established; thus, the application [of the argument] would serve merely to exclude that [yogic perception].
Furthermore, there might be the undesirable consequence that the Buddhists' proofs for [perception] being visual and so forth would also apply;
however, that specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) arises from the practice of yoga, asceticism, and the like.
Therefore, even that which is intended as "sage-like" (*ārṣa*) is included within that very same category, because it is not different in being produced by a preeminent unseen force.

As it is said in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*: "In this context, that cognition which manifests objects independently of the sense faculties is called 'divine' (divya); those who know the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) declare this to be a [form of] valid knowledge."
The supreme knowledge of the Lord, as well as the intellects of the liberated ones,
and even the inspired cognitions of sages such as Saṃjaya, Arjuna, and Vālmīki, are that [same reality].
Thus [it is said].
"Independent of the senses" means independent of the non-divine senses.
For this very reason, it is sung: "I give you divine vision," and so forth.
Alternatively, it should be understood in the same way from its being recited alongside [the knowledge of] the Supreme Lord and others.

And immediately after this it was said: "For innate cognition, which by its very nature illuminates all things, is obstructed by the veil of ignorance due to its connection with the senses; indeed, for liberated persons, there is no such obstruction of cognitions because of the destruction of ignorance."
By its own essential nature, it is the illuminator of all objects.
"The cognition of the sages, assisted by another factor that arises as its counter-activator, makes all things manifest once the state of obstruction has been removed."
Thus it is said.
The traditional teaching of the elders is that mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) does not exist even for people like us,
because the nature of the self and its attribute, knowledge, are self-luminous;
and because it has been established in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* that pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are not distinct from specific cognitions regarded as their respective causes.
This is because our experience of [the Self] as qualified by eternality and so forth is well-known from the scriptures and other sources;
because the cognition of previous experiences and the like takes the form of memory;

and because it is established—even by following the reasoning in the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa* commentary—that its activity toward external objects distinct from the self, pleasure, and so on, would be impossible without depending upon the external senses.
Consequently, non-yogic perception is the cognition produced by the external sense faculties.

It is generated by the sense organs assisted by factors such as universals (*sāmānya*), unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), light, and specific particulars; thus, due to the particularity of its causal complex, it has restricted objects.
It is fivefold, owing to the distinction between the unique causes of the sense faculties, such as the ear and the rest.
And the contact between the object and the sense-organ is as follows: in the case of substances, it is conjunction (*saṃyoga*);
but in the case of qualities such as color (*rūpa*) which reside in substances, it is the inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktāśrayaṇa*).
As it has been stated in the *Tattvaratnākara*: "In this regard, the elders have understood that proximity (*saṃnikarṣaṇa*) is conjunction."
And "resorting to that which is associated" should be inferred according to what is possible.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, perception is twofold: conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Perception accompanied by reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*) is conceptual;
perception devoid of that is non-conceptual.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 13.
The refutation of the Naiyāyika position on indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka).
Both of these types [of cognition] have only a qualified object as their domain.
This is because no cognition is observed, nor is it logically possible, that would apprehend an unqualified entity.
For even the consciousness of infants, the mute, animals, and so forth, although devoid of conceptualization through names (*saṃjñā-vikalpa*), has only a qualified entity as its object.

Otherwise, their activity preceded by the discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted would be untenable. A qualified cognition that is subject to dispute is preceded by the cognition of its qualifier,
because it is a qualified cognition.

If it is argued that [the cognition of the qualifier] is like the qualified cognition "fragrant sandalwood" and so forth, we say no; for in the case of qualifiers cognized by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), there is independence from that [qualifier-cognition],
since under the view of essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), the relation is grasped precisely through the grasping of the essential nature itself.
For the apprehension of the qualified object is established by that alone;

even in the theory of inherence (*samavāya*), that very [inherence] which is being apprehended constitutes the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), since it is accepted as being exactly so in the cognition of something qualified by inherence.
Furthermore, since the apprehension of the qualification of the quality is unavoidable when there is an apprehension of the qualification of that [substance],

it should not be argued that inherence (*samavāya*) is exclusively the object of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*); for in indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), the apprehension of that relation is possible, as its status as an object of sensory perception is no different from that of the attribute and the substratum.
Because it is impossible for a competent person who perceives a proximate relatum not to perceive the relation;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence that such a relation would never be perceived.
Thus, the cognition produced by the first contact of the sense-organ has a qualified object as its domain.
One should also consider such [arguments] as "because it is cognition, like that which is commonly accepted," and so forth.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 14.
An investigation of conceptual cognition.
Nor should it be said that conceptual cognition is not perception, because there is no difference in terms of its being a direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāra*) or its being unsublated (*abādha*).
Due to a specific auxiliary cause, a difference in genus (vaijātya) does not necessarily follow;
however, some degree of disparity may indeed occur within that same genus.
Wherever a difference in genus (vaijātya) is observed, it is accepted as such;
however, on that basis alone, this conceptualization should not be applied to all cases.
Nor is any cognition admitted to be produced by the sense-faculties alone;
for, due to specific auxiliary factors, they differ according to each individual faculty.
Therefore, even when there is a mixture of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), because it possesses the quality of immediacy (*aparokṣatva*),
the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) for conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) never ceases in any case.

The commentary beginning with "the apprehension of the first individual among objects of a single class is non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) should be understood as being intended merely as an illustration.
For this very reason, the venerable Viṣṇucitta stated: "Knowledge produced by the senses assisted by the awakening of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*);

whereas the apprehension of the first individual among objects of a single class, as well as the knowledge arising from the initial contact of the sense organ during the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals, is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)."
And it is stated elsewhere: "Non-conceptual [cognition] is produced solely by the sense faculties, such as the eye," and so forth.

As for what was stated in the *Tattvaratnākara*: “In non-conceptual [cognition], there is the exclusion of the qualifier’s own non-connection; in conceptual [cognition], the exclusion of its connection with another is likewise designated.”
Thus, even in that case, it should be understood that the intent is to demonstrate the independence from and dependence upon mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
And the classification of perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been stated as follows: "This perception is of two kinds: mundane (*arvācīna*) and supramundane (*anarvācīna*).
The supramundane is capable of the simultaneous direct intuition of all objects."
"That will be established as depending on the specific power of the liberated lords of yoga," and so forth.
For this very reason, the absurd claim of the proponents of false views—that perception grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*)—is refuted.
Furthermore, the critique regarding [the impossibility of] succession or simultaneity applies equally to erroneous conceptualization (*bhrānti-vikalpa*);
for even a conceptualization that is erroneous in nature, due to its momentariness, is incapable of functioning after having ceased.
Furthermore, one does not know the report of a prior cognition;
nor do you maintain that there is a grasping of difference in the absence of a self-grasping of the locus (*dharmī*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Nevertheless, if conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) were to grasp [the object] as qualified by difference all at once, [it would be untenable].
What death by a snake occurs in the case of direct perception?
Therefore, because it is as perceptible as the substratum itself, the distinction consisting of the forms of universals and so forth must also be grasped simultaneously.
Just like non-difference, difference also does not require a counter-correlative when it is cognized in its own nature.
The conventional usage of difference, like the conventional usage of non-difference, is dependent upon that [cognition];
therefore, it is logical that the cognition of difference occurs first.
For this very reason, the charge of mutual dependence regarding the cognition of property and substratum, or of substratum and counter-correlate, as well as other such cases, is refuted.

Consequently, even when there is linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based on that [notion of difference], there is no unwanted consequence [of it being a universal]. However, since usage with the word "difference" is mastered (*vyutpanna*) in a form determined by its counter-correlate (*pratisambandhin*), it depends upon that [counter-correlate].

For the state of being a difference (*bhedatva*) of individual differences is determined by their counter-correlate, and not by an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) characterized as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
For when the apprehension of something X contradicts the superimposition of Y upon it,

X is indeed the difference of that [X] from that [Y]; and since the universal "cowness" and so forth, when being apprehended, precludes the superimposition of "horseness" and so forth upon itself and its own substratum, it is thus the difference of itself and its own substratum from that [horseness] by its very nature.

Furthermore, by asserting that the apprehension of identity is impossible because of the difference [between objects] characterized by the superimposition of contradictory properties—namely, dependence on a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) versus independence from one—you are proving difference for the very purpose of refuting difference; thus, there is a contradiction with your own words.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 2, Verse 15.
Refutation of the Directness of Verbal Cognition.
They themselves describe that there is also perception produced by words;
however, that too is incorrect because it involves a contradiction.
For a causal complex (sāmagrī) established as having the nature of producing something beyond the senses would not, in the absence of any specific distinction, ever deviate from its own nature.
Furthermore, an effect produced from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of a single nature could not be diverse,
because it would follow that all types of things could arise from that very same complex, and because it would follow that a single effect would possess contradictory natures.
Even in the illustrative example, "You are the tenth," only the referent of "you" (*tvam-artha*) is perceptible.
For the cognition "I am the tenth" does not arise through the independence of the sense organ,
but rather in accordance with the words of another person;
if even that which is rooted in such [testimony] were considered direct perception, [then all testimony would be so].
Likewise, when one understands from the instruction of an astrologer, "You possess such-and-such qualities," that "I am like that," it would follow that even those qualities are directly perceived.
Consequently, nothing in the world would be non-perceptual,
because everything could be established as perceptual simply by being a qualifier with respect to something already directly perceived.

However, in the case of instructing a person who has already ascertained the tenth state (the Self), there may or may not be for some the empirical usage of "immediacy" regarding the cognition produced by the intermediate words— due to the uninterrupted sequence of preceding and succeeding perceptions— following the maxim of ink dropped into a mass of words. For this very reason, the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and so forth generates a perceptual knowledge whose object is its own referent.
Inferences such as "because [the Veda] has as its object an immediately present thing, like the sentences ‘You are the tenth’ or ‘Consciousness is self-luminous’" have been refuted;
for it is unestablished that, in the case of the examples, an immediate cognition is produced in a qualified form characterized by being the tenth, self-luminosity, and so forth.
Likewise, the disputed word does not produce a perceptual cognition whose object is its own denotation.
One should also employ counter-arguments such as: "Because it is sound, like that which is commonly agreed upon," and so forth.

In this case, the subverting argument against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*) is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that there would be a contradiction with perception, a conflict with verbal testimony, and a confusion of the definitions [of the means of knowledge].
This is not the case for the former [position],

because the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) occurs through direct intuition produced by yoga-born merit even without perception generated by words, or through the volition of the Supreme Self when propitiated by a specific act of mental concentration.

We desire to behold that Wise One, who is skilled in the method of bestowing liberation upon those who have attained him—he of whom it is heard that this world, composed of consciousness and unconsciousness, is his very self; he whose infinite glory becomes manifest to those of undistracted minds; and he alone by whom this entire universe is eternally and simultaneously made visible from his own being.

Thus ends the second section in the chapter on perception within the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians and the independent master of all systems of thought.
And thus concludes the chapter on perception.
Salutations to the illustrious Great Preceptor of the Vedānta.
